steps.body: One rule has worked quietly under every comparison so far: **both fractions described the same whole** (or same-size wholes). Break it and comparisons collapse — 1/2 of a blueberry is far less berry than 1/4 of a watermelon. Before comparing, always ask: *of WHAT?*
Referee duty: which matchups are legal?

widget.prompt: Sort each matchup: fair comparison, or meaningless?

items.label: 3/8 vs 5/8 of the same cake
items.feedback: One cake, one whole — a legal fight (5/8 wins it, same pieces, more of them).

items.label: 1/2 of a small cup vs 1/3 of a big jug
items.feedback: Cup and jug are different wholes — the jug's third could drown the cup's half. So you cannot tell which is bigger.

items.label: 2/6 vs 2/3 of two same-size ribbons
items.feedback: Same-size ribbons count as matching wholes — legal (and 2/3 wins: same tops, bigger pieces).

items.label: 3/4 of my sticker vs 3/4 of your poster
items.feedback: Same NAME, different amounts — three-quarters of a poster dwarfs three-quarters of a sticker. Matching fractions still need matching wholes.

widget.missFeedback: Check the WHOLES first: same object or same-size objects → fair; different sizes → you cannot tell.
widget.successFeedback: The cake and the twin ribbons are legal fights; the cup-vs-jug and sticker-vs-poster matchups are meaningless — mismatched wholes.

predict.prompt: Half of a small cookie versus half of a big cake — the same amount?

options.label: Yes — a half is a half

predict.reveal: A fraction is a share OF something — big whole, big half. Comparing fractions only means anything when the wholes match.

explanationVariants: A fraction is a share OF something — a fourth of a poster and a fourth of a sticky note are the same NAME on very different amounts.
1/4 of an hour and 1/4 of a year are both fourths, and nowhere near the same length.

widget.prompt: Marta says: '1/4 of my sticky note equals 1/4 of your poster — a fourth is a fourth!' Is she right?

options.label: Not necessarily — a fourth's amount depends on the whole it comes from
options.feedback: Same fraction, different wholes, different amounts. The name matches; the stuff doesn't.

options.label: Yes — 1/4 always equals 1/4
options.feedback: The FRACTIONS match, but fractions measure shares OF a whole — and these wholes are wildly different sizes.

options.label: Her sticky note's fourth is the bigger one
options.feedback: The note is the SMALL whole — its fourth is the smaller piece. Bigger whole, bigger fourth.

options.label: Fractions don't have sizes at all
options.feedback: They do the moment you name the whole: 1/4 of THAT poster is a real, measurable amount.

steps.body: So when CAN you compare? **Same object, same-size objects, or the same 0→1 trip on one number line.** That's the line's superpower — it forces every fraction onto one shared whole. The pre-comparison ritual is two words: *of what?*

explanationVariants: 1/2 > 1/4 is only true of ONE whole — a family-size fourth can out-feed a mini half. With mismatched pizzas, you cannot tell.
Fractions compare shares, not food, unless the wholes match — and these don't.

widget.prompt: Leo ate 1/2 of a MINI pizza; Ana ate 1/4 of a FAMILY-SIZE one. Leo says: 'I ate more — 1/2 beats 1/4!' What's wrong?

options.label: The pizzas aren't the same size — a family-size fourth could easily be more food than a mini half
options.feedback: 1/2 > 1/4 compares shares of ONE whole. Different pizzas, so you cannot tell — Leo's rule fired outside its territory.

options.label: Nothing — Leo wins
options.feedback: His rule needs matching wholes to fire. A mini pizza's half can be a couple of bites; a family fourth can be dinner.

options.label: Ana definitely ate more
options.feedback: Careful — that claim breaks the same rule! Without knowing the sizes, NEITHER side can be decided.

options.label: Fractions can't describe pizza
options.feedback: They describe pizza beautifully — one pizza at a time. It's the cross-pizza comparison that needs matching wholes.

steps.body: The full toolkit, one last drill.

widget.prompt: Match each matchup to its correct answer — all three chapter rules are in play.

left.label: 1/2 of a cup vs 1/2 of a pool

right.label: Cannot tell — the wholes don't match
5/6 wins — same pieces, more of them

pairErrors.feedback: The tops match, but a cup and a pool are different wholes — you cannot tell for that matchup, however tempting the counting.

widget.missFeedback: Ritual first — 'of what?' Then: same bottoms count tops; same tops favor the smaller bottom.
widget.successFeedback: Same-pan counting, same-bar piece sizes, and one illegal matchup thrown out — the full referee's toolkit.

steps.body: The rule, stated once and forever.
explanationVariants: Comparisons need one shared measuring stick — the same whole, or wholes of equal size.
That's why the number line settles fights: it forces both fractions onto a single 0→1 whole.

widget.prompt: Two fractions can be fairly compared only when…

options.label: They describe the same whole, or same-size wholes
options.feedback: One shared whole is the measuring stick every comparison stands on.

options.label: Their top numbers match
options.feedback: Matching tops is one handy CASE (piece size decides) — but even it silently requires matching wholes first.

options.label: Their bottom numbers match
options.feedback: Also just one case (count decides) — and it too leans on the wholes matching underneath.

options.label: Both are smaller than 1
options.feedback: Size doesn't matter — 5/4 and 7/4 compare fine (same whole, same pieces). Mismatched WHOLES are the only dealbreaker.

steps.body: The trail mix showdown — the whole course in one puzzle.
hints: Referee first: whose bags are the same size?
Kim vs Raj is legal — same-size bags, same tops (2 each).
Nia's jumbo bag is a different whole — what does that do to her matchups?
explanationVariants: Kim vs Raj is the only legal fight (identical bags): same tops, and thirds beat fifths — Kim ate more. Nia's jumbo bag is a different whole, so you cannot tell for either of her matchups.
Ritual, then rules: 'of what?' throws Nia's comparisons out; the surviving duel falls to the same-top rule, 2/3 > 2/5.

widget.prompt: Kim ate 2/3 of her small bag of trail mix; Raj ate 2/5 of his — their bags are identical. Nia ate 3/4 of a JUMBO bag. Which comparisons have real verdicts?

options.label: Only Kim vs Raj — and Kim ate more (2/3 > 2/5); Nia's jumbo bag breaks her matchups
options.feedback: Matching bags make Kim–Raj legal: same tops, thirds beat fifths. The jumbo bag is a different whole — nothing can be decided about Nia.

options.label: All three — just compare the fractions
options.feedback: Fractions only compare on a shared whole. Kim–Raj share one (twin bags); Nia's jumbo doesn't — her matchups are thrown out.

options.label: None — the fractions all differ
options.feedback: Differing fractions are exactly what comparisons are FOR. Kim vs Raj is legal (matching bags) and has a clean winner: 2/3 > 2/5.

options.label: Nia ate the most for sure — 3/4 is the biggest fraction
options.feedback: Biggest FRACTION, unknown amount — of a different whole. 3/4 of a jumbo bag can't be ranked against the small bags without sizes.

takeaways: Ask 'of what?' first — no verdict without matching wholes.
Same bottoms: count the tops. Same tops: the smaller bottom wins.
Fair cuts, honest names, one shared whole — that's the entire fraction game.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Before ANY comparison, ask two words: **"of WHAT?"** Half a raisin loses to a fourth of a melon — the fraction names a share, and the whole sets the share's size. Matching wholes, or no match at all.

explanationVariants: A juice box and a barrel are different wholes — their fractions can't be ranked against each other.
The barrel's third could fill dozens of juice boxes — 'of what?' throws this matchup out.

widget.prompt: Can you fairly compare 1/2 of a juice box with 1/3 of a barrel?

options.label: Not fairly — the wholes are different sizes
options.feedback: Mismatched wholes, so you cannot tell — the referee's whistle blows.

options.label: Yes — 1/2 beats 1/3
options.feedback: That rule works on ONE whole. A barrel's third holds far more juice than a box's half.

options.label: Yes — the barrel's 1/3 wins
options.feedback: Probably true about the juice — but it isn't a FRACTION comparison anymore; it needs the actual sizes. As fractions, you cannot tell.
